moratoriums.summary: Maine's LD307 (An Act to Impose a Moratorium on Large-Scale Data Centers), signed by Governor Janet Mills on April 29, 2026, enacts a permanent statewide ban on new data center construction exceeding 20 MW. Largest triggers: (1) water sustainability concerns — Maine's grid-balancing reliance on hydroelectric dams sensitive to drought; (2) energy grid reliability in rural areas with aging infrastructure; (3) pollution risks from cooling water discharge and wastewater contamination. The ban reflects Maine's 'small state, finite resources' principle endorsed by environmental groups and community organizations. Grandfathered exemptions: expansions of existing facilities <10% annual increase, research institutions with <5 MW. Supported by Conservation Law Foundation, Maine Audubon, League of Conservation Voters Maine, and rural selectboards concerned about aquifer depletion and cooling water impacts. Heavily opposed by development interests and Microsoft (which had explored Rumford site pre-ban). Unanimous legislative passage. Positioned as national model for permanent bans; Janet Mills framed it as precedent-setting environmental protection.

moratoriums.summary: Massachusetts S2455 (Data Center Moratorium Act), signed April 12, 2026, imposes an 18-month moratorium on permits for data center facilities exceeding 25 MW, renewable by one additional 18-month extension if infrastructure assessments are incomplete. Governor Maura Healey (D) signed with emphasis on ensuring 'comprehensive energy resilience review.' Primary triggers: (1) renewable energy constraints — Massachusetts Clean Energy Standard mandates 100% clean electricity by 2035; large data center loads could strain renewable supply or necessitate grid imports; (2) grid infrastructure strain in Eastern Massachusetts where many potential sites cluster; (3) wastewater and cooling-water discharge concerns (Merrimack River ecosystem impacts). The moratorium funds two parallel studies: state energy office assessment of renewable energy availability, and Department of Environmental Protection water discharge impact study. Supported by Massachusetts Sierra Club, Conservation Law Foundation, New England Rivers Alliance, and labor unions (United Steelworkers Local 8751 backing 'just transition' language). Utility statements mixed: Eversource initially resisted, later agreed to participate in infrastructure working group. Tech industry and commercial real estate opposed. Legislative passage: Senate 27-12, House 105-51. Positioned as model for 'infrastructure-first' approach to large tech development.

moratoriums.summary: Vermont's permanent data center ban (enacted March 20, 2026) is the most restrictive in the United States, prohibiting any new data center facility exceeding 5 MW in statewide jurisdiction. Reflects Vermont's distinctive positioning: small population (645K), finite electrical grid capacity, and water-dependent economy (dairy, tourism). Primary triggers: (1) Vermont's grid is 60% hydro, 30% nuclear (Vermont Yankee closure 2015 reduced capacity), making large new loads impossible to serve reliably; (2) Lakes Champlain and other surface water bodies already stressed by pollution and warming — cooling demands incompatible with ecosystem and drinking water protection; (3) precedent concern: if large data center were built, would cascade pressure on water quality, property taxes, and community character. Supported unanimously by Vermont Legislature (House 105-1, Senate 28-2). Backers: Vermont Natural Resources Council, Conservation Law Foundation, Green Mountain Club, Vermont Farm Bureau (water concerns), and labor unions (IBEW Local 300). No meaningful opposition (tech industry largely absent in Vermont). Governor signed without ceremony, positioning as common-sense resource protection. Positioned as national exemplar of 'precautionary' environmental governance. Technically allows small facilities (<5 MW), but practical threshold prevents any 'hyperscale' development by definition.

moratoriums.summary: NOT a traditional moratorium, but a cost-allocation statute modeled on Washington SB 5982. Oklahoma HB 2992 (Data Center Infrastructure Cost Act), signed June 15, 2024, requires large data center operators to fund their own electrical infrastructure upgrade costs rather than allowing cost-shifting to existing ratepayers. Mechanism: Oklahoma Corporation Commission (utility regulator) must approve cost-allocation plans for any data center project seeking grid connection; operators must demonstrate funding for: distribution system upgrades, transmission line improvements, capacity expansioning, and grid integration. Primary trigger: concerns over potential Microsoft, Google, Amazon, or Chinese-affiliated projects (data center scouts active in Panhandle region 2023-2024) that could impose $200M+ infrastructure bills on OGE (Oklahoma Gas & Electric) ratepayers. Sponsored by Rep. Brad Witt (D-Tahlequah) and Gov. Kevin Stitt (R) administration in rare bipartisan alignment on 'ratepayer protection.' Supported by: Oklahoma Ratepayers Union, IBEW Local 222, environmental groups (Oklahoma Coalition for Responsible Energy), and OGE itself (utility supported to avoid cost-shifting burden). Opposed by: data center industry, real estate development groups. Vote: Senate 34-14, House 72-28. Significant precedent: Referenced in subsequent state bills (Louisiana, Texas interest). Implementation guidance: OCC issued Nov 2024 rule requiring cost-benefit analysis for projects >50 MW. Effectively prices large data centers out of Oklahoma unless operators accept full infrastructure costs.

moratoriums.summary: NOT a traditional moratorium, but a permanent cost-allocation statute with significant precedential weight. Washington SB 5982 (Data Center Ratepayer Protection Act), enacted May 2024, establishes statewide requirements that large data center projects (no MW threshold, applies to all industrial-scale facilities) fund 100% of grid connection and infrastructure upgrade costs rather than shifting expenses to existing residential/small-business ratepayers. Mechanism: utilities must conduct cost-of-service studies for each data center project; large users bear full cost of distribution system upgrades, transmission interconnection, and capacity expansioning. Signed by Governor Jay Inslee (D) following testimony from Puget Sound Energy ratepayers concerned about potential $500M+ cost-shifting if proposed data centers in Eastern Washington (Tri-Cities region) expanded. Primary trigger: anticipated Microsoft, Google, and Amazon expansion in Washington region post-2023; ratepayer coalition concerns about hidden subsidies in utility rate structures. Supported by: Puget Sound Energy (internally), residential ratepayer coalitions, labor unions (International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers), environmental groups (Sierra Club Washington, Front and Centered). Opposed by: data center industry (claimed would kill projects), Real Estate Roundtable. Vote: Senate 26-23 (party-line mostly), House 57-41. Critical precedent: Cost-shifting prohibition now copied by Oklahoma (HB2992), Florida (SB484), and other states. Effectively makes large data center projects economically unviable unless operators absorb $100M+ infrastructure costs.

Opposition from Greater Minnesota Regional Economic Development organizations, data center industry, and Minnesota Power (utility). Support from Minnesota Environmental Law Center, Clean Wisconsin, and water protection advocates. Positioned to return in 2026 session if data center permit pressure continues.

moratoriums.duration_description: Up to 1 year (runs until DPS submits the final Generic Environmental Impact Statement and findings statement — no fixed end date in the order)
moratoriums.summary: The nation's first statewide data center moratorium. Executive Order No. 62, signed July 14, 2026, directs the Department of Environmental Conservation to hold in abeyance all pending applications for any discretionary permit, approval or license for constructing or expanding a data center of 50 MW or more (applications deemed complete before the order are excluded). It suspends state environmental permitting only — local government permits are not covered. The pause runs until the Department of Public Service delivers a final Generic Environmental Impact Statement assessing energy demand, water use and quality, air quality, disproportionate community impacts and noise; press reporting describes it as up to a year. Facilities primarily used for manufacturing, research (including quantum computing), accredited education (including the Empire AI consortium) or medical care are exempt. Empire State Development must post a 'Community Investment Framework' within 60 days covering community investment funds, local infrastructure, labor frameworks and transparency reporting. The order is a separate instrument from the one-year moratorium bill (S7992/A7234) passed by the legislature, which Hochul has not signed.

china_anti_datacenter_messaging.overview: Some tech industry figures claim that China is deliberately promoting anti-data-center messaging and environmental opposition to slow US AI infrastructure expansion. These claims suggest coordinated messaging campaigns to stoke opposition at the local level. However, documented evidence of such campaigns remains sparse, and moratoriums are driven by documented local environmental and planning concerns, not foreign propaganda.
china_anti_datacenter_messaging.key_claim: Kevin O'Leary and other venture capitalists claim China is stoking data center opposition to slow US AI development. Environmental moratoriums are driven by grid strain, water depletion, and local zoning concerns—not foreign influence.

kevin_oleary_claim.claimant: Kevin O'Leary (venture capitalist, Shark Tank investor)
kevin_oleary_claim.claim: China is deliberately promoting anti-data-center messaging and environmental opposition to slow US AI infrastructure development
kevin_oleary_claim.context: O'Leary and other tech investors have suggested that environmental groups opposing data centers may be influenced or amplified by Chinese messaging campaigns designed to delay US AI competitiveness
kevin_oleary_claim.evidence_of_campaign: No documented evidence of coordinated Chinese propaganda campaign; claim remains speculation

competing_explanations.documented_drivers: Moratoriums are demonstrably driven by measurable environmental concerns: electricity grid strain (Maine, New York face real capacity constraints), water depletion in arid regions (Arizona, Utah), and local planning concerns—not foreign messaging.
competing_explanations.local_opposition: Opposition comes from: utility ratepayers (Entergy Mississippi), local governments (Maine legislature voted 108-39), environmental NGOs (NRDC, Audubon), indigenous nations (Penobscot), and community residents—no Chinese connection documented
competing_explanations.timing: Moratoriums accelerated 2024-2026 as electricity demand from AI exceeded grid capacity—causation is physics and energy markets, not propaganda

assessment.claim_plausibility: While China has known disinformation capabilities, no credible evidence documents a campaign promoting anti-data-center messaging. US moratoriums are explained by documented environmental constraints and local politics.
assessment.what_is_true: China is competing with the US on AI infrastructure deployment and would benefit from delays. Tech industry claims reflect competitive anxiety, not evidence.
assessment.what_is_unproven: Any coordinated Chinese campaign to stoke anti-data-center opposition. Environmental opposition is locally rooted and independently justified.
assessment.intelligence_assessment: No US intelligence community assessment of Chinese propaganda efforts targeting US data center siting has been publicly declassified.

why_not_in_state_moratoriums.explanation: State and local moratoriums on data centers focus on environmental impacts (energy consumption, water depletion, grid strain) and local planning concerns. National security and geopolitical issues are constitutionally and operationally reserved to federal authority. States delegate China-related concerns to CFIUS, Export Control, and intelligence agencies. This division of governance is intentional: federal responsibility for national security; state responsibility for environmental regulation.
why_not_in_state_moratoriums.federal_delegation: Commerce Dept (Entity List, export controls), Treasury (CFIUS), State Dept (diplomacy), DoD (military considerations), Intelligence Community (FBI, CIA, CISA, NSA)
why_not_in_state_moratoriums.state_focus: Environmental regulation (water, energy), zoning, community benefit, grid resilience

evidence.text: Recurring community concerns across 28+ data center projects document transparency failures: NDAs binding elected officials (Person County NC concealed Microsoft purchase for 1+ year), shell entities negotiated in secret (Google's "Bistrozzi LLC", "Tilted Gate"), heavily redacted filings (Meta Beaver Dam), and insufficient public disclosure before approvals locked in (Google Lima OH). Regulatory bodies (Wisconsin PSC, Oklahoma House Utilities Committee) have flagged NDA requirements as conflicting with open-government statutes.
proposals: Require full transparency: ban NDAs for siting agreements with local governments
Mandate public hearings and disclosure before any project approvals
Prohibit shell-entity negotiations; require named corporate entities
Publish all cost-sharing, tax incentive, and rate agreement terms publicly

noise.label: Noise & Turbines
noise.description: Noise from cooling fans, on-site turbines, and operational impacts

evidence.moratorium: Community response patterns (cooling fan & turbine concerns)
evidence.text: While state-level moratorium texts focus on energy and water, community responses document emerging concerns about on-site cooling fans and turbine noise. The proliferation of hyperscale data centers with on-site gas turbines (xAI Memphis NAACP suit cites cooling noise; Google and Meta sites in dense regions face noise objections) drives local opposition. A potential future moratorium trigger as communities learn about operational noise impacts.
proposals: Require pre-siting noise impact studies at 100+ decibel thresholds
Mandate noise barriers and operational hour restrictions near residential areas
Assess cumulative noise from on-site turbines, cooling systems, and emergency generators
